title: Establishing, and tearing down, a connection
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe what happens before connect() returns, read a connection's state from a running system, and recognise the two states that indicate a bug.

blocks.text: connect() looks instantaneous. It is not — three messages cross the network before it returns, and a similar exchange happens at the end. Those states are visible on any running machine, and two of them are how you find a whole class of server bug.

blocks.caption: What happens inside connect()
lines: /* Three messages, so establishing a connection costs one full round trip
before any data moves. On a 100 ms link that is 100 ms of latency you
pay before sending a single byte — which is why connection reuse matters
so much, and why the second curl in the first lesson was faster. */

blocks.text: Both sides also agree on where their byte numbering starts, which is what lets the receiver detect gaps and reorder what arrives. The starting numbers are chosen unpredictably, because a predictable choice would let an attacker who cannot see the traffic inject data into it.
The states, seen on a real machine

blocks.caption: Observed with netstat while a server ran
lines: # and across the whole machine at that moment:

rows: This side closed first and is waiting before releasing the address
The peer closed; this side has not called close()

blocks.text: Closing takes four messages, and is asymmetric

Each direction is closed independently. One side says it has no more to send; the other acknowledges and may keep sending. Only when both directions are closed is the connection finished. This is why a socket can be readable after you have stopped writing to it, and why 'the client disconnected' does not automatically mean you may stop sending.

blocks.title: CLOSE_WAIT that accumulates is always your bug
blocks.text: It means the peer closed, your program was told — read() returned 0 — and it never called close(). The connection sits there holding a descriptor forever. A machine showing a large and growing number of them has a program that is not closing sockets, and the fix is always in that program, never in the kernel. Thirteen were present on the machine used for this lesson, which is a normal background level for a desktop but would be a warning sign on a busy server.

blocks.title: TIME_WAIT is not a bug, and you should not try to remove it
blocks.text: The side that closes first waits before releasing the address, so that any delayed packets from the old connection cannot be delivered to a new one that reuses the same address and port. Verified: a connection from this lesson's test sat in TIME_WAIT after both programs had exited. It is also why restarting a server needs SO_REUSEADDR — the option from the previous lesson exists precisely to work with this state, not against it.

rows: Nothing is listening on that port
A firewall dropping silently, or the host is down
Routing or an interface is down
The peer crashed, or a middlebox closed it

blocks.text: The difference between refused and timed out is the most useful diagnostic distinction here. A refusal proves the packet reached the machine and something rejected it — a fast, honest answer. A timeout proves nothing reached anything that would reply, which points at filtering rather than a missing service.

blocks.title: Watch the states change
steps: Start a server that accepts and then sleeps for 30 seconds before closing
In another terminal: watch -n1 'ss -tan | grep <your port>'    (or netstat -an | grep <port>)
Connect a client and watch the state go from nothing to ESTABLISHED
Close the client first and watch which side shows TIME_WAIT
Now close the server first instead and confirm TIME_WAIT moves to the other side
Write a server that accepts and then never closes; connect and disconnect a client, then look for CLOSE_WAIT
Connect to a port nothing is listening on and note how fast the refusal is
Connect to a filtered address (for example a public IP on a closed port) and note the timeout instead
blocks.expected: A connection you watched move through its states, TIME_WAIT appearing on whichever side closed first, and a CLOSE_WAIT you created on purpose by omitting close(). That last one is the skill worth having: recognising in a production listing that the bug is a missing close, and knowing it is in the program rather than the network.

cheatsheet: Establishing takes three messages — one full round trip before any data
That round trip is why connection reuse and keep-alive matter
Starting sequence numbers are unpredictable, to prevent blind injection
Closing takes four messages and closes each direction independently
LISTEN and ESTABLISHED are normal; SYN_SENT is normal briefly
TIME_WAIT is normal: the side that closed first waits before releasing the address
SO_REUSEADDR exists to work with TIME_WAIT, not around a bug
CLOSE_WAIT that accumulates means your program is not calling close()
Refused = something answered no. Timeout = nothing answered at all

checkpoint.prompt: A server shows hundreds of connections in CLOSE_WAIT, and the number keeps rising. Where is the problem?
checkpoint.explanation: The peer closed, it was told, and it never called close() CLOSE_WAIT means the local side has been informed and has not responded by closing. Each one holds a descriptor, so the count only rises until the program runs out.

checkpoint.prompt: Connecting to one address is refused instantly; connecting to another times out after 30 seconds. What does the difference tell you?

choices.B: Both mean the service is down
choices.C: The refusal reached the machine and got an answer

checkpoint.explanation: The timeout means nothing that would reply was reached, which points at filtering A refusal is a fast honest answer and proves reachability. A timeout proves only silence, which is what a firewall configured to drop rather than reject produces.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does establishing a TCP connection cost a full round trip before any data moves?

choices.A: Three messages must cross before either side may send data

checkpoint.explanation: On a link with meaningful latency this is paid before a single useful byte. It is the reason connection reuse and keep-alive make such a visible difference.

checkpoint.prompt: Should you configure the system to eliminate TIME_WAIT?

choices.B: No — it prevents delayed packets from an old connection being delivered to a new one on the same address and port

checkpoint.explanation: It is a correctness mechanism. SO_REUSEADDR exists so that a server can restart while it is present, which is working with the state rather than removing it.
